questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted the destination to be further away from Denmark to get out of my comfort zone and also be able to travel to places I normally wouldn't go.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I received a lot of information via email from the Global Programs team at The Australian National University. Before arrival they held a few zoom meetings and sent out powerpoints on what do before and after arrival and really made an effort to make sure that you didn't miss any information regarding visas, accommodation and also on how to physically get there in the smartest way.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They held in person presentations during orientation week where you could meet other exchange students and ask questions, etc. It was always possible to reach out to the Global Programs team during the stay and their response time was quick.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of different options for housing in different price ranges. I stayed in a 6 person bedroom dorm which was cheaper but 1-5 person dorms were also available.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were some accommodations with meal plans. I did not stay at an accommodation with meal plans as I thought it was a bit too expensive and I probably wouldn't recommend it if you think you will travel a lot while there. I had a kitchen in my 6 bedroom apartment that I did not use much but my roommates liked it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Some housings are a lot more social than others (like Fenner, Burgmann, Wamburun). If you choose to live in postgraduate housing with no undergraduate students you can expect it to be more quiet (for example: Toad Hall). I would recommend looking at the social media of the different housing offers and even looking up on tiktok what people actually living there have to say about it. Send your application for housing well in advance as I think I was a little late with my application. I was very lucky with the people who were staying in my 6 dorm bedroom but something to consider is that if you are staying at a UniLodge accommodation, there are a lot of monthly cleaning checks where you need to pass which can be difficult if you are staying with roommates who don't know how to clean and then have to pay for a professional cleaner to come out. Also, if you get offered a one year contract for half a year and they give you a short deadline to accept the offer but you need to have it amended and there isn't time to have it changed, you can just accept the contract and have it changed to half a year later - happened to a lot of people at UniLodge.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to submit an application to receive course codes to be able to sign up for the courses you wanted. There was a course catalogue for available courses. I found it slightly confusing because there were some 'prerequisites' for each course. For example to be able to take a specific law course, for some you need to have had an introduction course to Australian institutions which wasn't available during my semester. But when you submit the request for the course codes, you can submit documentation detailing that you have had a similar course back home which gives you the same requisites to take the course you want. For this documentation I submitted the course descriptions in English for KU courses I had previously taken. When I had received the course codes, I could register for the course on their ISIS portal. For some courses you have to sign up for tutorials and you should pay close attention to when that sign up opens, because the classes fill up quickly and you might not get the specific weekly time/date you want.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Global Programs team do send out very detailed guides on the registration process and checklists, so you should can on that.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registered for all the classes I wanted but I know that a lot of people were waitlisted for different courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you want to drop or swap a course at the start of the semester, think about the fact that there may not be a lot of other courses with available spots or available tutorial classes - so check the availability for a course you want to swap to before your drop the courses you already have. It is your responsibility to make sure that you are registered for enough classes in order to not lose your visa.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Three of my courses were MA level and then it was a requirement by the host institution that I take a BA course on introductions to Australian law. Even though it was a BA course, however, I was graded as an MA student and during assignments I had to write more words. I think you can decide yourself if you wish to be in the BA or MA group but check with KU during your course approvals as they may have an opinion.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There were participation requirements for a lot of the courses. The grading was more spread out with like 10% for participation, 30% for a group presentation, 60% for a research essay or 50% for a research essay and 50% for a sit-in exam. There were some exam assignments during mid-term and some during the end of the semester. It varied between courses how much time the course convener spent lecturing and the amount of group work/active participation. Some of the courses had lectures and some only had seminars.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Foundations of Australian Law: it's an undergraduate class you are required to take during their semester 1/our spring term. There was a one hour lecture each week (which was also recorded and uploaded later) and a two hour tutorial like classic two hour seminars back home. The examination was a paper worth 50% that had to be submitted after the semester break and a 45% hand written 90 minute sit in exam at the end of the semester. The last 5% was class participation points. You were allowed two tutorial skips and then you also had a presentation to do where you had to visit an Australian Court and talk about it for 3 minutes in class.

Chinese Law and Society: postgraduate course. We were around 170 people in the class which was a lot of people for a seminar class. There was a 3 hour seminar each week and a 3 hour pre-recorded lecture. The course convener was super nice and very well educated on the topic. He would usually spent the first half of the class lecturing and then the rest was group presentations. You had to do a group presentation with 3 other people which was worth 20% of your grade. For the group presentations, you need to be aware that the majority of the class participants are Chinese international students who sometimes will only speak in Chinese at the table even if you are also sitting there, so if you do not want to feel left out and want to be able to communicate with your group members, consider joining a group of Australian students. I signed up for the group presentations before the semester started. As there were so many students, the way the teacher did participation points was by making a survey you could join and register participation and do a little quiz each time - you did not actually have to say anything. You could also even join the survey if you for some reason were sick and couldn't be there if you left the tab open from the last time. The last part of the examination was a research essay worth 70%. It was a little bit difficult finding sources and the relevant legislation as some of the legislation isn't translated into English so keep this in mind. The teacher was very helpful in providing ways to find sources and even sent me some legislation that I didn't have access to. 

International Humanitarian Law: postgraduate course with one two-hour seminar a week. Great teacher. She sometimes did the seminar via zoom. The examination was 10% participation (you had to say stuff during class but didn't have to be there every time, I didn't really do that but still got an alright grade), 30% was a research proposal (you had to write a short proposal on what you wanted to write the subsequent research essay on). The 30% research proposal was handed in around 1,5 months into the semester and then the actual research essay worth 60% was handed in at the end of the semester.

Information Technology Law: postgraduate and undergraduate course. There were no participation requirements for this class. 50% was a research essay that had to be submitted a bit after the semester break and then an online problem exam worth 50%. He did some of the seminars on zoom. It was one 3 hour seminar per week and he recorded the seminars and uploaded the recordings afterwards.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you want to do a bit of traveling during the week and would like as much flexibility as possible, I would recommend international humanitarian law and information technology law so you have the option of skipping some classes. Also, there were very nice classes with good teachers and interesting material. International Humanitarian Law is not very difficult when you have already had international law and IT law was a nice mix between intellectual property rights, cybercrime and AI.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spent a lot of money on traveling each month while I was on exchange which I have not accounted for in the numbers above. I also did not really cook and mainly ate out or got takeaway, especially as I travelled a lot. I spent a lot on plane tickets and accommodation and activities. The above numbers would more likely reflect a normal month in Canberra.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The food and especially coffee was less expensive compared to Copenhagen. You could get very cheap sushi rolls. Transport was not vert expensive either, especially if you travel to the Queensland state where all transport is 1 Australian dollar. I did not expect to have to pay 2000 DKK (a one time amount) for a mandatory overseas health insurance when I was already paying around 500 DKK pr month for a private Danish travel insurance. The cost of domestic flights can be surprisingly expensive sometimes, because the distances are a lot further than you think. It's a good idea to buy plane tickets early in advance.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: During orientation week, the university hosts a market day where all of the associations and clubs are available at their stands so you get an idea of what you can join.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There were so many associations that offered different social activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I took a lot of weekend trips to different places. You can easily take a three hour Murray's or Greyhound bus to Sydney. You can fly to Melbourne or Tasmania. There is a 2 week semester break where I went to New Zealand. After exams I did a 3 week roadtrip from Cairns to Byron Bay. I also took a trip to Fiji and a lot of people travelled to Bali or Western Australia during the break. You can try and plan the travels according to the weather as the temperatures are very different across australia. In Canberra, there were a lot of hiking opportunities and nice restaurants and historical buildings. I would recommend a visit to the Parliament, the High Court, the War memorial, Mount Ainslie, the Botanical Gardens, Mount Majura Vineyard or going to watch a rugby or AFL game. You can also take a two hour bus to Batemann's Bay or Wollongong by the ocean or rent a car and go to Jervis Bay, which is an old military base and has very nice water and sand.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was a pretty easy adjustments as Australians in general are a more welcoming people. It took a while getting used to receiving so many questions about how my day had been at the supermarket.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join some clubs.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Students are a lot more willing to participate in class discussions so if you want to get some participations points, you need to make a bit of an effort.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness of Australian people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Use your free time to travel. There is also a lot to see in Canberra even though the reputation is that it is boring and the university is great. It will be expensive, so apply for grants.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: For accommodation, make sure to look up the different housing options and do some thorough research. Apply for student housing in good time as well. For courses, make sure to sign up for tutorials when the opportunity opens (Australian time) as you might get waitlisted if you are not quick enough.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Gaining more confidence by having to be very independent.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The few times I was feeling unwell were a bit tough so definitely important to surround yourselves with good people and have a good relationsship with your roommates, they really helped a lot.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
